_nota: 1 ago 2026. Guion escrito para PROBAR CHATTERBOX, no solo para cumplir reglas. Por eso lleva un recorrido emocional amplio a proposito -- rabia (el email de las dos de la manana) -> verguenza -> duelo -> ternura -- que es justo donde un TTS plano como edge-tts se delata y donde el control de exageracion de Chatterbox tiene algo que hacer. Cumple igualmente 9 (hecho afirmado, sin resolver: amenace con demandarla y luego le mande flores), 9f (cold open sobre la consecuencia + rebobinado), 9g (premio en el segundo 8, cero relleno). Giro fair-play: la pista es que ella contesta en once minutos a las dos de la manana y renuncia al cobro sin discutir -- solo tiene sentido si ya sabia. El reencuadre final cae sobre el padre, no sobre ella. Loop: cierra en la tarjeta de las flores y encadena con 'le mande flores' de la primera frase.
script: I threatened to sue my wedding photographer, and eleven months later I sent her flowers. The gallery came back three weeks after the wedding. Fourteen hundred photos. Not one of them had my father in it. Not one. He walked me down the aisle. He sat at the top table. He danced with my mother for the first time in nine years. Fourteen hundred photographs, and he is in none of them. I wrote her an email at two in the morning that I am still ashamed of. I used the word negligent. I used the word refund. I told her I would be speaking to a lawyer. She wrote back in eleven minutes. At two in the morning. She said, I understand. I will not be charging you for the day. That should have told me something. It did not. My father died in March. Nine weeks after the wedding. And in April a package came with no note in it, just a memory card and one printed sheet. Fourteen hundred and six photographs. All of him. Him fixing his tie in the hallway. Him crying in the car park before he came in, which nobody saw. Him and my mother. And the one where he is watching me from the side of the room and does not know the camera is there. The printed sheet was an invoice. Paid in full. Four hundred and fifty dollars, in his handwriting at the bottom, dated three weeks before the wedding. He had known since January. He asked her to keep them out of the main gallery and hold on to them, because he did not want my wedding album to be the album where everybody goes looking for him. He wanted me to have a wedding first. And then, later, to have him. She carried that for eleven months and let me call her negligent. I sent flowers. I still have not worked out what the card should have said.
